Memory? Well... I suppose that depends on what you mean, doctor. If you mean, do I forget where I put my reading glasses? Sure, I do that. But who doesn't at my age? I'll set them down on the side table by my chair when I go to fetch the newspaper, and then I'll spend ten minutes looking for them in the kitchen. Mary always finds them right where I left them and gives me that look she has. You know the one. 

But my real memory? The important things? No, that's sharp as a tack. I can tell you the starting lineup for the '55 Dodgers, clear as a bell. I can tell you exactly what the weather was like the day Mary and I got married—it was unseasonably warm for October, and the leaves were just starting to turn that bright orange down by the creek. I remember the smell of the wood shavings at the mill like I was just there yesterday.

A head injury? Or a stroke? Oh, goodness, no, doctor. The Good Lord has spared me from all that, thankfully. I mean, I have my everyday aches and pains, sure—like I mentioned about my stiff knees taking a while to get going—but nothing serious like a stroke or a seizure. As for hitting my head, well, I haven't had a bump on the noggin since... oh, it must have been the spring of '72. We had this terrible thunderstorm roll through, knocked a heavy oak branch right onto the gutters, and like a fool, I got up on the old aluminum ladder while the ground was still soft. The ladder slipped right out from under me in the mud. I came down hard and whacked my head on the stone birdbath. Mary came running out the screen door with a dish towel and a bag of frozen peas, hollering that I was going to be the death of her. 

But I haven't done anything foolish like that in a long, long time. When you get to be eighty-four, doctor, you learn to take things slow. You have to, really. You rush around, you trip on a throw rug, and the next thing you know you've broken a hip and you're lying in a hospital bed catching who-knows-what from the other patients. Hard to follow? Making sense? Well, doctor, I wouldn't say that at all. Not at all. I mean, sure, sometimes Mary will give me that look—the one I told you about, where her eyebrows go all the way up to her hairline—and she'll say, "Arthur, what on earth are you going on about now?" But that's just Mary. She's got her mind on her knitting patterns or the price of ground chuck at the A&P, and she just isn't paying attention to the bigger picture. 

I speak perfectly clearly, if you ask me. I take my time, I lay out all the facts, just like I'm doing with you right now. You have to explain things properly, don't you think? If you just give a yes or no, people miss all the important details. Like the other day, I was down at the hardware store—the one on Elm Street, not the big new one out by the highway, I don't care for that one, it's too bright and the aisles are too wide, it doesn't smell like a hardware store should—anyway, I was talking to young Jimmy behind the counter about the right kind of nails for fixing a loose board on the back porch, and I was explaining to him how the wood swells in the humidity we've been having. I told him all about how the weather patterns have been changing, and how it ties into those messages I've been picking up on, the ones the government is sending through the television static. Jimmy just stared at me with his mouth half open, like a fish out of water, and then he said, "Mr. Higgins, I just need to know if you want galvanized or not." 

But that's not me being hard to follow, doctor. That's just young people today. They don't have the patience to listen to a full thought. They want everything in a hurry, zip-zip-zip, on those little phones they're always staring at. If they'd just slow down and listen to how all the pieces connect—the weather, the wood, the static, the warnings—they'd see it makes perfect sense. So no, I don't think I'm hard to understand. People just aren't trying hard enough to understand me.

Lost interest? Well... I suppose it's not so much losing interest as it is... just not having the energy for it all anymore. I still love my family, doctor, don't get me wrong. He used to be in the church choir years ago, and he had this real deep voice, and I will hear him humming a choir song out there. \n\nI will push myself up out of my chair, which takes some doing these days with my stiff knees, and I will shuffle over to the window to look out. I try to tell Mary when she wakes up. I tell her my friend was just out there humming, but she just shakes her head and tells me I was dreaming. But I was wide awake, doctor. You do not just imagine a choir tune coming through the wood of your own front door, plain as day.\n\nDoctor: Have you been drinking alcohol heavily lately?\n\nPatient: Alcohol? Oh, no, no, doctor. I haven't been a drinking man for... oh, it's got to be decades now. I mean, sure, when I was a younger fella, back when I was working at the mill, the boys and I would sometimes head down to O'Malley's after a long shift. You know how it is when you're young and got a bit of change in your pocket and the dust from the day still in your throat. We'd have a beer, maybe two, just to unwind before heading home to the wives. But even then, I was never one to overdo it. My father, rest his soul, he had a bit of a heavy hand with the bottle, and I saw what that did to my mother, so I always kept a tight lid on it myself. \n\nAnd lately? Heavens, no. My stomach just wouldn't tolerate it these days anyway. Between the heartburn and the way my digestion acts up if I even look at something too spicy, I can't imagine pouring liquor down there. So, no, doctor, no heavy drinking here. Just a cup of weak coffee in the morning and maybe some ginger ale in the afternoon if my stomach is feeling unsettled. My mind is perfectly fine, just... busy, I suppose. Busy with all those messages and warnings I told you about. I mean, I have my everyday aches and pains, sure—like I mentioned about my stiff knees taking a while to get going—but nothing serious like a stroke or a seizure. Confused about where I am? Oh, no, no. No, doctor, I know exactly where I am. I've lived in the same house on Elm Street for, oh, it must be fifty-two years now. Mary and I bought that place right after the youngest was born. It's a sturdy house, you know, built back when they actually cared about the framing. Like I said before, when you're not punching a clock down at the plant every morning, the days do tend to blur together a bit. Mary keeps a big calendar on the refrigerator, one of those ones with the large print from the pharmacy, and she marks off the days with a big red X. So if I ever need to know, I just look at the fridge. But it's not like I wake up thinking it's 1985 or anything like that. I know it's the present day, I know who the president is—though sometimes I wish I didn't, if you catch my drift—and I know I'm sitting right here in this office with you. 

I suppose the only time I ever get a little turned around is... well, maybe when I'm listening to my friend humming out on the porch. Sometimes, just for a split second, it feels like we're back at choir practice, getting ready for the Easter service. But that's just a feeling, you know? A memory washing over me. I still know I'm in my own house. I still know it's whatever day Mary has marked on the calendar. My mind is sharp enough for that, doctor. I may not have had much schooling—I had to leave after eighth grade to help my father on the farm, you know how it was back then—but I've always had a good head on my shoulders for the practical things. She doesn't understand that they're warning me. They're telling me I need to be careful, that I need to watch my back. I try to explain it to her, I really do, but she just waves her hand and tells me I'm being foolish. But a man knows when he's being spoken to, doctor. A man knows.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever hear voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Well, now that you ask about it... yes, I suppose I do. But it is not just some stranger making noise, doctor. I will be sitting there in my chair, maybe just resting my eyes for a minute, and I will hear him call my name right from the front porch. Arthur, he says, just as clear as day. It is so clear, it is exactly like he is standing right there on the welcome mat, just waiting for me to come unlatch the screen door. And if he is not calling for me, he is humming. He used to be in the church choir years ago, and he had this real deep voice, and I will hear him humming a choir song out there. \n\nI will push myself up out of my chair, which takes some doing these days with my stiff knees, and I will shuffle over to the window to look out. I fully expect to see him leaning against the porch railing, but when I pull the curtain back, there is nobody out there. Not a soul. Just the empty porch and the street. I try to tell Mary when she wakes up. I tell her my friend was just out there humming, but she just shakes her head and tells me I was dreaming. But I was wide awake, doctor. You do not just imagine a choir tune coming through the wood of your own front door, plain as day.\n\nDoctor: Have you been drinking alcohol heavily lately?\n\nPatient: Alcohol? Oh, no, no, doctor. I haven't been a drinking man for... oh, it's got to be decades now. I mean, sure, when I was a younger fella, back when I was working at the mill, the boys and I would sometimes head down to O'Malley's after a long shift. You know how it is when you're young and got a bit of change in your pocket and the dust from the day still in your throat. We'd have a beer, maybe two, just to unwind before heading home to the wives. But even then, I was never one to overdo it. My father, rest his soul, he had a bit of a heavy hand with the bottle, and I saw what that did to my mother, so I always kept a tight lid on it myself. \n\nAnd lately? Heavens, no. So, no, doctor, no heavy drinking here. Just a cup of weak coffee in the morning and maybe some ginger ale in the afternoon if my stomach is feeling unsettled. That's about the strongest thing I put in my body.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble with your memory lately?\n\nPatient: Memory? Well... I suppose that depends on what you mean, doctor. I'll set them down on the side table by my chair when I go to fetch the newspaper, and then I'll spend ten minutes looking for them in the kitchen. Dementia? Alzheimer’s? Oh, heavens no, doctor. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I see Dr. Higgins down at the family clinic—have been seeing him for, oh, it must be twenty-something years now, ever since old Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida. Anyway, Dr. Higgins gives me a full workup every single year right around my birthday in October. He checks the blood pressure, listens to the heart, taps the knees with that little rubber hammer... and he always makes a point to ask me those silly questions to test the memory, you know? 

He'll ask me to remember three words, like 'apple, table, penny,' or something like that, and then we talk about my cholesterol for ten minutes, and then he asks me to repeat them back. I always get them right, every time. I tell him, 'Doc, I might have had to leave school in the eighth grade to help my daddy run the farm, but there’s absolutely nothing wrong with my memory.' And he just laughs and says my mind is as sharp as a tack for a man my age. 

I mean, sure, I might forget where I set my reading glasses down from time to time. Just last Tuesday, I spent half the morning looking for them, turning the living room upside down, and wouldn't you know it, they were sitting right on top of the morning paper on the kitchen counter the whole time. Mary had a good chuckle about that, told me I'd lose my head if it wasn't attached to my neck. But who doesn't get a little forgetful about the small things at eighty-four? That’s just normal wear and tear, isn't it? It’s not a disease. 

Mary might call me stubborn as a mule, and she sure doesn't like me talking about hearing Thomas out on the porch, but she knows my mind is sound. She trusts me to balance the checkbook every month, and I never miss a penny. So no, no Alzheimer’s or dementia or anything of that sort. Just an old man with old joints and a perfectly good memory.

I told him all about how the weather patterns have been changing, and how it ties into those messages I've been picking up on, the ones the government is sending through the television static. Jimmy just stared at me with his mouth half open, like a fish out of water, and then he said, \"Mr. Higgins, I just need to know if you want galvanized or not.\" \n\nBut that's not me being hard to follow, doctor. That's just young people today. They don't have the patience to listen to a full thought. They want everything in a hurry, zip-zip-zip, on those little phones they're always staring at. If they'd just slow down and listen to how all the pieces connect—the weather, the wood, the static, the warnings—they'd see it makes perfect sense. So no, I don't think I'm hard to understand. People just aren't trying hard enough to understand me.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest in seeing people or doing things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Lost interest? Well... How old was I? Well, let me think on that for a second, doctor. I’m eighty-four now, and like I mentioned, my birthday is in October. So if we count backwards... well, the voices and those special messages, they've been happening on and off for about nine months now. So I would have been eighty-three. Yes, eighty-three.

Mary has been threatening to throw that chair out or get it reupholstered for the better part of a decade, but I won't let her. A man gets used to his chair, you know? It molds to you over the years, and it fits me perfectly. 

Anyway, I was eighty-three, sitting right there in that chair, reading the afternoon paper, when the messages first started coming through. It wasn't just a hum anymore, it was real words, real messages. And like I said, it’s been on and off for nine months since then. Not every single day, mind you. Sometimes I'll go a few days or a week and it's quiet, just the birds outside at the feeder and Mary clattering around in the kitchen with her baking pans. But then, sure enough, they come back. It's funny how things change on you when you least expect it. You live in a house for fifty-two years, sit in the same chair, read the same paper, and then one afternoon when you're eighty-three, everything is just a little bit different.

I figured I was just missing him so much that my brain was filling in the silence with his voice. \n\nBut it didn't stop. It just kept happening. And it's so clear, doctor. I know they say when people pass on, they go to Heaven and they're at peace, but sometimes I wonder if Thomas just... didn't quite make it all the way there. So maybe he's coming to me, bringing the music to my back porch. Mary says I'm letting my imagination run away with me, that I need to let him rest in peace, but how can I do that when he's right there, humming \"The Old Rugged Cross\" as clear as day? It's been a year and five months, doctor, and he hasn't stopped visiting yet.\n\nDoctor: Has any doctor ever told you that you have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease?\n\nPatient: Dementia? Alzheimer’s? Oh, heavens no, doctor. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I see Dr. Higgins down at the family clinic—have been seeing him for, oh, it must be twenty-something years now, ever since old Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida. Anyway, Dr. Higgins gives me a full workup every single year right around my birthday in October. He checks the blood pressure, listens to the heart, taps the knees with that little rubber hammer... and he always makes a point to ask me those silly questions to test the memory, you know? \n\nHe'll ask me to remember three words, like 'apple, table, penny,' or something like that, and then we talk about my cholesterol for ten minutes, and then he asks me to repeat them back. Mary had a good chuckle about that, told me I'd lose my head if it wasn't attached to my neck. But who doesn't get a little forgetful about the small things at eighty-four? That’s just normal wear and tear, isn't it? It’s not a disease. \n\nMary might call me stubborn as a mule, and she sure doesn't like me talking about hearing Thomas out on the porch, but she knows my mind is sound. She trusts me to balance the checkbook every month, and I never miss a penny. So no, no Alzheimer’s or dementia or anything of that sort. Just an old man with old joints and a perfectly good memory.\n\nDoctor: How old were you when these messages and voices first began?\n\nPatient: How old was I? Sometimes I'll go a few days or a week and it's quiet, just the birds outside at the feeder and Mary clattering around in the kitchen with her baking pans. But then, sure enough, they come back. It's funny how things change on you when you least expect it. You live in a house for fifty-two years, sit in the same chair, read the same paper, and then one afternoon when you're eighty-three, everything is just a little bit different.\n\nDoctor: Have you been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease?\n\nPatient: Parkinson’s? No, doctor, no. Nobody has ever mentioned Parkinson’s to me. My hands are just as steady as they ever were. Dr. Higgins told me years ago that arthritis is just the price we pay for living a long life and working hard with our hands. And I did work hard, doctor. Forty years at the plant, plus all that time on my daddy's farm before that, hauling hay and fixing tractors. Seeing things? Oh, no, no. My eyes aren't what they used to be, like I was saying about losing my reading glasses, but I don't see anything that isn't there. No ghosts or shadows walking around the living room, nothing silly like that. But... well, hearing things, now, that’s a bit different.

Sometimes, just for a split second, it feels like we're back at choir practice, getting ready for the Easter service. But that's just a feeling, you know? A memory washing over me. I still know I'm in my own house. I still know it's whatever day Mary has marked on the calendar. My mind is sharp enough for that, doctor. I may not have had much schooling—I had to leave after eighth grade to help my father on the farm, you know how it was back then—but I've always had a good head on my shoulders for the practical things. I know exactly where I stand.\n\nDoctor: Is the old friend whose voice you hear someone who has died?\n\nPatient: Well... yes. Yes, he is. That's... that's the thing of it, doctor. That's why Mary gets so upset when I mention I've been listening to him out on the porch. \n\nHis name was Thomas. Thomas Miller. We knew each other for... oh, it had to be sixty years. We worked at the plant together, our wives were in the same garden club, and of course, all those years standing shoulder-to-shoulder in the choir loft. He was a good man, Thomas was. The kind of man who would give you the shirt off his back and then apologize that it wasn't ironed. \n\nHe passed away... well, it's been about a year and five months now. It was sudden, you know. Heart just gave out on him while he was out pulling weeds in his tomato patch. One minute he was there, and the next he was gone. It was a terrible shock to all of us. Mary baked three casseroles that week just to keep her hands busy, and I... well, I just sat in my chair and stared at the wall for a good long while. \n\nAnd then, not too long after the funeral... maybe a few weeks, a month at most... that's when it started. That's when I first heard him humming on the porch. It's been going on ever since, for this whole year and five months. At first, I thought my mind was just playing tricks on me, you know, grief doing what grief does. I figured I was just missing him so much that my brain was filling in the silence with his voice. \n\nBut it didn't stop. It just kept happening. And it's so clear, doctor. I know they say when people pass on, they go to Heaven and they're at peace, but sometimes I wonder if Thomas just... didn't quite make it all the way there. Or maybe he just misses the choir as much as I do. I haven't been back to church since he died, you see. It just doesn't feel right standing up there without him. So maybe he's coming to me, bringing the music to my back porch. Mary says I'm letting my imagination run away with me, that I need to let him rest in peace, but how can I do that when he's right there, humming \"The Old Rugged Cross\" as clear as day? It's been a year and five months, doctor, and he hasn't stopped visiting yet.\n\nDoctor: Has any doctor ever told you that you have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease?\n\nPatient: Dementia? Alzheimer’s? Oh, heavens no, doctor. No, nobody has ever said anything like that to me. I see Dr. Higgins down at the family clinic—have been seeing him for, oh, it must be twenty-something years now, ever since old Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida. Anyway, Dr. Higgins gives me a full workup every single year right around my birthday in October. He checks the blood pressure, listens to the heart, taps the knees with that little rubber hammer... and he always makes a point to ask me those silly questions to test the memory, you know? \n\nHe'll ask me to remember three words, like 'apple, table, penny,' or something like that, and then we talk about my cholesterol for ten minutes, and then he asks me to repeat them back. I always get them right, every time. I tell him, 'Doc, I might have had to leave school in the eighth grade to help my daddy run the farm, but there’s absolutely nothing wrong with my memory.' And he just laughs and says my mind is as sharp as a tack for a man my age. \n\nI mean, sure, I might forget where I set my reading glasses down from time to time. Just last Tuesday, I spent half the morning looking for them, turning the living room upside down, and wouldn't you know it, they were sitting right on top of the morning paper on the kitchen counter the whole time. Mary had a good chuckle about that, told me I'd lose my head if it wasn't attached to my neck. But who doesn't get a little forgetful about the small things at eighty-four? That’s just normal wear and tear, isn't it? It’s not a disease. \n\nMary might call me stubborn as a mule, and she sure doesn't like me talking about hearing Thomas out on the porch, but she knows my mind is sound. She trusts me to balance the checkbook every month, and I never miss a penny. So no, no Alzheimer’s or dementia or anything of that sort. Just an old man with old joints and a perfectly good memory.\n\nDoctor: How old were you when these messages and voices first began?\n\nPatient: How old was I? Well, let me think on that for a second, doctor. I’m eighty-four now, and like I mentioned, my birthday is in October. Yes, eighty-three. \n\nNow, I know I told you earlier that I started hearing Thomas humming on the porch a month after he passed, which was over a year ago. That started about nine months ago. Mary has been threatening to throw that chair out or get it reupholstered for the better part of a decade, but I won't let her. A man gets used to his chair, you know? It molds to you over the years, and it fits me perfectly. \n\nAnyway, I was eighty-three, sitting right there in that chair, reading the afternoon paper, when the messages first started coming through. It wasn't just a hum anymore, it was real words, real messages. And like I said, it’s been on and off for nine months since then. Not every single day, mind you. Sometimes I'll go a few days or a week and it's quiet, just the birds outside at the feeder and Mary clattering around in the kitchen with her baking pans. But then, sure enough, they come back. It's funny how things change on you when you least expect it. You live in a house for fifty-two years, sit in the same chair, read the same paper, and then one afternoon when you're eighty-three, everything is just a little bit different.\n\nDoctor: Have you been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease?\n\nPatient: Parkinson’s? No, doctor, no. Nobody has ever mentioned Parkinson’s to me. My hands are just as steady as they ever were. Well, I mean, I get a little stiffness in the knuckles first thing in the morning, especially when the weather turns cold and damp like it does around late November, but that’s just the arthritis talking. Dr. Higgins told me years ago that arthritis is just the price we pay for living a long life and working hard with our hands. And I did work hard, doctor. Forty years at the plant, plus all that time on my daddy's farm before that, hauling hay and fixing tractors. You use your hands that much, they're bound to ache a bit when you get to be eighty-four. \n\nBut they don't shake. Not like that Parkinson’s. I knew a fellow once, old Charlie Henderson, who used to run the hardware store downtown before those big box stores moved in and pushed him out. Charlie got the Parkinson’s real bad in his later years. It was a crying shame to see, really. He’d try to count out your change at the register and his poor hands would tremble so much the nickels and dimes would just clatter right onto the counter. He had to have his daughter come in and run the till for him eventually, and you could tell it just broke his pride in two. \n\nBut me? No, nothing like that. I can still pour a cup of black coffee right to the brim without spilling a single drop, and just last week I helped Mary thread a needle because her eyes get tired in the evening when she's trying to mend my socks. Just the regular old creaks and groans of an old machine, that's all.\n\nDoctor: Have you been seeing things that other people cannot see?\n\nPatient: Seeing things? Oh, no, no. I know the exact way he hums those old hymns. Just the empty porch and the hanging ferns. So no, I don't see anything unusual, not a single thing. But I sure do hear him.\n\nDoctor: Have you been diagnosed with any major medical illness, such as a brain disease or another serious health condition?\n\nPatient: Major medical illness? Brain disease? Oh, no, no, doctor. Goodness, no. Nothing like that. Like I said, I've got the arthritis in my hands, and my knees aren't quite as spry as they were back when I was climbing up on the tractors, but that's just normal wear and tear. No, nobody has ever told me I have a brain disease or a tumor or... or whatever else might be serious like that. \n\nI mean, I go to see Dr. Higgins—well, it's Dr. Higgins' son now, young Dr. Higgins, since the older one retired and moved down to Florida. Energetic? Less sleep? Well, now, that is an interesting question, doctor. Because Mary was just fussing at me about this very thing not two weeks ago. Usually, you see, we have our routine. We watch the Wheel of Fortune, maybe catch the ten o'clock local news, and then it's off to bed. But every now and then... I don't know what gets into me, but I'll have these spells. They might last three or four days, sometimes near on a whole week, where my body just decides it doesn't need the pillow at all. On those nights I may sleep only two or three hours, then get up before daylight feeling ready to work like I had a full rest. 

It is the strangest thing, doctor. I'll lay my head down at ten, and by one or maybe half-past one in the morning, my eyes will just pop wide open. Wide open! And I'm not tossing and turning or feeling groggy, either. I'll feel so full of vinegar I can't just lay there staring at the ceiling, so I have to get up and do something. I'll go down to the kitchen, being real quiet on the stairs so I don't wake Mary, and I'll start finding chores. 

Last time it happened, I took apart the toaster to clean out all the burnt crumbs from the bottom, and then I got out my tools and oiled every single hinge on the kitchen cabinets. Mary came down at six in the morning in her pink robe, turned on the light, and just stared at me sitting there on the floor with a screwdriver. She said, "What on God's green earth are you doing up?" But I tried to tell her, I just didn't need the sleep! I felt fantastic. Back when I was working on the line at the plant, I would have paid good money to feel that spry for a morning shift. I could have worked a double shift and still had energy to mow the lawn. So yes, I do get those days where I just don't need much shut-eye at all and feel completely raring to go.

Well, powers... I don't know if I'd call it magic powers, like you read about in comic books or see in those superhero movies the grandkids watch. It's a powerful feeling, let me tell you, knowing you're the one who holds the key to fixing how disconnected everyone's gotten.
